Then you climb — up the cleared floor, past the dead Sentinel's rubble, to the arch at the head of the stair the guardian died holding — and you go through it carefully, the Furnace-heart raised before you for its dim red light.

Beyond the arch, the floor falls away. There is no floor. You stand at the lip of a vast black shaft that climbs and drops past any light you carry — a lightless throat of the Tower with cold air sighing up out of the depths, dust and old grease on its breath — and far, far above, so high it might be a star, a single thin seam of grey: the way out. Stairs climb the wall in broken bolted flights, some fallen away into gaps; and past where the stairs give out there are SLABS — great flat stones rising and sinking through the dark on a slow, steady beat, passing each other on no machine you can see. You nudge a chip of rock off the lip. It falls, and falls, and you never hear it land. A fall here is not a hurt. It is the end.

And you are not alone in it. Somewhere up in the moving gaps between the slabs, something LIVES — you hear it before anything else: a dry shift of weight, a breath that is not the wind, circling in the black where your small light cannot reach. Then it goes silent, and strain as you might you cannot find it, cannot see it. It hunts the dark, and the dark is everything here, and your eyes were never your strength. But your mind is. Crouched at the lip with the core's glow in your fist, you read the whole shape of it cold: this floor belongs to the thing in the black, and the one thing that takes it back is LIGHT. And there — wedged in the wall at the first broken landing, within a careful reach — a guttered lantern-bracket and a sealed flask of oil, sitting just where a climber would want them. Light first. Then the moving stones and their patient beat, and the long fall under every leap.

You have not set a foot past the lip. You have only looked, and listened, and understood. The way up is a dark mouth with a hunter in it and a single lamp waiting to be lit — and you crouch at the threshold of it, a warm mace in one hand and a banked coal in the other, having learned the shape of the dark without yet stepping into it.

You decide the dark mouth itself is the place to learn. You will not climb into it — better to meet whatever lives up there here, at the lip, with footing under you, than higher where a wrong step is the end. So you plant yourself at the threshold and begin to practice.

Small. As small as you can pinch a thing of fire and still send it. You flick a bead of emberlight up into the black and it sails and pops against far stone, and for a heartbeat a patch of the shaft stands lit — then dark again. Another, smaller, steadier; another. Spot by patient spot you paint the lower throat of the shaft out of the black and hold it in your head: the first broken flights bolted to the wall and the gaps where they have fallen away; the nearest slabs rising and sinking on their slow regular beat; and there at the first landing, just where you read it from the threshold, the guttered bracket and the sealed flask of oil waiting to be lit. Your control tightens as you go — the bolts coming smaller, truer, costing you less to place exactly where you want them.

And you test the three ways of throwing them. Direct, from your own hand, they are sharpest and come the instant you will them — but each one is paid out of you. Pushed through Burning Anger they leap far and bright, the mace flinging fire across the dark like a thrown brand — but fat and crude, and you feel its bound warmth bleeding out fast under the work; it is a flare-thrower, not a candle. Pushed through the Furnace-heart they come steady and clean and cost you almost nothing — the core feeds them out of its own banked fire, cooling slowly as it pays, and you understand you could light this dark for a long, long time this way. Three tools. You file each one where you can reach it.

You are still working when the dark changes its mind about you.

All this while the thing up in the shaft has been circling, idle, a dry shift of weight at the edge of hearing. Now it stops circling. Now it comes. Whatever it is, it has felt your little suns and your warmth blooming over and over at the threshold, and it is done watching — the sound of it firms into purpose and begins, deliberately, lower and nearer, to close on the warm thing standing in its doorway. You snap a bolt toward the sound, and for one white instant the light catches it: a long pale low shape, close to the stone, eyes throwing your glare back flat and bright — and it FLINCHES, recoiling from the brightness before it pours itself back into the black and keeps coming. The light hurts it. You know that now, bought with a single glimpse.

It is almost on you. You crouch at the lip you chose to hold — the re-bound mace low in one fist and its charge near spent, the dimming core in the other, two-thirds of your focus still in you — with a hunter you cannot quite see closing the last of the dark between you, and the entrance you meant to defend at your back. You wanted to meet it here. Here it comes.

It comes. In the last of the dark it gathers and lunges for the warm thing in the doorway — and you give it exactly what you have been holding back. You do not meet it in the open; you have stepped back into the throat of the entrance, where the stone closes in around you and there is nowhere for it to slide aside, nowhere to flank. You wait the half-breath until it commits its whole long body into the gap — and then you open the Furnace-heart's last fire through your own and throw it all forward at once: one broad wash of Ember poured into the doorway with nowhere to go but through it.

Let's see how the night likes meeting the sun.

The night does not like it at all. There is no dark here for it to be — the fire fills the choke wall to wall and the creature is caught full in the open flame with no slot to pour itself into, and the light does to it what light does to a thing built for the dark. It comes apart. The wave takes it head-on and flings the ruin of it back into the shaft, the pale shape blackening and breaking in the glare, and the long body that meant to kill you out of the dark falls away from your doorway dead before a single claw ever reaches you.

Then the fire gutters down and the dark slides back in — quieter, now, than it was. Whatever you feared up here is gone; you feel it in the air, the hunted prickle lifting off the back of your neck. By the last dim coal in your fist you can make out the wreck of it slumped against the broken stair: a long lean carcass, a tough pale hide stretched over too many ribs, and where its eyes should be, two clouded lenses that seem to drink the little light you have rather than throw it back. Strange salvage, if you want it.

The core in your other hand has gone dark and cold. You spent its last in the wave — an empty stone now, no glow left to give. You have your low-charged mace, your own fire, and the dark above you still to climb.

And the Tower marks the kill.

You crouch over the wreck of the thing and take what is worth taking. The hide peels away light and tough under your knife, pale as something that has never seen a day; and from the ruin of its face you work loose the two clouded lenses that were its eyes — cold little stones that swallow your coal light instead of catching it, strange enough that you pocket them. Then you get a grip on what is left of the carcass and haul it up onto your shoulder.

Down you go, the way you climbed, back through the dead quiet of the cleared rooms — past the Sentinel's rubble, down to the low warm dark by the water where your brazier stands. You let the carcass down by the stone and straighten, and take stock of the place you have made your own these long turns: the cistern with Cold Revenge soaking in it, the heaped salvage, the iron hammer-head still wanting a haft — and the brazier itself, cold. Dead cold. You burned the last of your fuel the night you forged yourself, and there is nothing left in the basket but old ash. Whatever you mean to do here, one last time, before you leave these rooms for the long climb — the forge is dark, and the fire to do it by is not yet lit.

There is no preparing anything over a dead hearth, so you go and find fire's food. Down the cleared flights to the first floor — the bottom of all this, where you started — and you work it over slow and thorough, turning up what a hundred climbers and your own earlier passes have left: a broken stool gone to splinters, the dry guts of something wooden long collapsed, a drift of brittle debris in the corners that takes a flame. It is not a woodpile, but it is real fuel, more than you hoped to find in a place so picked-over, and you bundle the best of it up and haul it back up to the water and the cold brazier — an armful for the fire, and a little over to keep.

You build it up properly this time: the foraged wood stacked in the basket and the coil of rotted rope laid through it for tinder, and then you call a seed of your own Ember down into the heart of it the way you can now without a flint or a spark to beg from. It catches. The rope crackles and the old wood takes and the brazier wakes into real flame, throwing live orange light across the water and the stone — the first proper fire you have had since the night you forged your flesh.

Into it you set your three fire-things. The Furnace-heart, dark and spent, you bed down in the coals with a seed of essence in it; the little rivet beside it, the same. And this time the mace goes in too — for it is bound again, not the dead iron it was that cold night, and when you give it its seed the head drinks the heat and holds it, its low charge beginning to climb. All three sit in the fire now, drinking, their charges rising as the pyre burns down through your fuel. The forge is alive again, the leftover wood stacked dry at your side, and the work you came down here to do is waiting on whatever you decide it is.

Before the fire does its slow work you do yours. You sit by the pyre and take up the three points the Tower gave you for the kill, and you spend them the way you like to — one at a time, slow, feeling for where each one lands.

The first you press into your PRESENCE, an attribute you have let lie. It answers oddly — not in the flesh like strength but in the air around you: a small added weight to the way you sit here, the sense that were anyone in this dark to look, their eye would catch and hold on you a beat longer than before. You file the lesson away — that this one governs how a person fills a room and leans on the minds in it.

The second you give to LUCK, the lowest thing on your sheet, and this is the strangest of the three, because it is almost nothing you can hold. No filling, no weight — only the faintest sense, gone before you can name it, that the world's million small coin-flips might fall a hair more often your way than they did a moment ago. Fortune's thumb, set the barest touch lighter on the scale. You take it on faith more than feeling.

And the last you set where you are already strongest — your INTELLECT, building the high thing higher. This one you feel cleanly: a widening behind the eyes, more room to hold a thing and turn it, and under it the cool well of your focus going deeper, a little more of you to spend before you run dry. The points are placed. You sit sharper, weightier, and a touch luckier by the fire, your three fire-things still drinking the flame beside you and the work itself still ahead.

You will not be back, and you cannot carry it all, so you stop being careful with what you can spend and start being curious instead. The cold bar first. You lift Cold Revenge dripping from the cistern, set both hands to it, and pull — not into an item this time but into yourself, drawing its cold charge in through your skin the way you drew the rivet's fire that day by the water.

It comes in WRONG. Where the ember came home smooth, a thing your body knew and wanted, this is the opposite of welcome — a hard, biting essence that does not belong in you, that fights up the channel and tries to bleed back out the moment it is in. A lesser grip would have let it shock through you and freeze something it should not. But you have the hands for it now: you hold the cold steady, thread it slow and deliberate through the meat of you, and make it show you exactly what it does.

What it does is nothing that lasts. For as long as you push it the flesh goes numb and stiff and strange, a brittle false hardness — and the instant you stop feeding it, it is gone, draining away like water through a fist, leaving not a grain set behind. Your body will not take the cold. The fire it took because the fire was already yours, the same single note your essence has always rung; the cold is the other pole, a thing you can hold in your hand and put into iron but never into the man. Ember already hardened in you everything essence can harden. There is nothing here the cold can add. You let the last of it bleed off, shake the chill out of your fingers, and set the drained bar down — answered, and none the worse for asking. Cold Revenge is an empty cold-husk now, to refill in the water if you want it; and you know one true thing more about what you are.

The rivet has drunk its fill. You lift it from the coals where it has sat since you built the pyre, and it comes up hot and heavy and FULL, a small iron sun you can close in one fist, its bound ember pressing at the shell of it and wanting out. The pitted hammer-head waits on the stone beside it. You have forged before with open flame driven up under the metal; this time you mean to forge with the charge itself, and see what that changes.

It works at once. You set the rivet to the iron and open its binding a careful crack — not pulling the ember into yourself, not throwing it, only letting it RUN OUT into the head as working heat — and a deep even orange blooms up from the contact and races through the mass faster than any brazier ever drove it. A thing the size of a knuckle is running your forge. So: it can be done.

And it is easy on you, which is the surprise. The rivet pays for the fire; your own well barely stirs, where keeping an open channel lit always cost you to hold. All you spend is the fine will to meter the charge, to keep it from dumping itself all at once. But you feel the other edge of it too — the rivet is EMPTYING under your hand, a purse with the coins leaving it, and when it is spent the heat is simply gone. Open fire is endless while the fuel lasts. This is cheap and it is bounded, both at once.

The real thing you did not expect is what the ember does while you hammer. It does not only heat the iron and pass through. Every blow that shapes the head drives a little of that ember DOWN into it and SETS it there — the same way your own essence set into Burning Anger long ago, only here it is the smithing itself doing the binding. The head is not just getting hot. It is getting BOUND, a faint new ember-quality waking in the worked metal and taking hold. You ease off with your heart going, because you see what you have stumbled into: that the hammer and the binding are not two crafts but one, that a tool could be made ember from the inside out. The head cools half-shaped in your grip, faintly alive now with a fire that is partly its own — still a bare head, still wanting a haft, no longer only iron. The rivet in your other hand is an emptied husk, its whole charge poured into the work.

You have one thing left to spend and a use for it, so you spend it. Kneeling at the pyre with the last of your focus cool and low in you, you set to binding — pushing your own ember out of yourself and down into iron, the way you have learned to, only now you do three at once and do not stop to rest between them.

The hammer-head first, to finish what you started. The nascent ember you woke in it before is still there, half-set; you take it the rest of the way, drive the fire down into the grain and seat it, and feel the head go from iron-that-holds-some-warmth to a thing that is ember in its bones — done, bound, only wanting a haft. The brazier-stand next, the old iron basket that has held your every fire: it takes the bind easy and grateful, same as your own pole always does, and you feel it learn to keep a coal of its own and wake its own flame.

Then the cold bar — the one that was Cold Revenge, that you bit with the swarm's cold and have carried ever since. This one fights you. The old cold-bind is still in it, the other pole, and when your ember goes in the two grind against each other like wrong-cut gears. But the cold was only ever a crude grip, a thing that bled and needed water to hold at all, and your fire is HOME in iron — so you simply pour harder, and the ember does not negotiate with the cold so much as BURN IT OUT, scouring the old binding loose and taking its place clean. The bar goes from a thing that bites cold to a thing that holds your fire, and you understand a new edge of what you are: that you can walk into a crude opposite bind and evict it, make it yours. The cold is gone out of it. It is an ember rod now, like everything else in your hands.

That is the last of your focus, and you let it be. You heap what fuel you have left onto the brazier — the whole remainder, holding nothing back — and you set every ember thing you own into it: the mace, the rivet, the new-bound head and rod, the brazier-stand alight under all of it, and the Furnace-heart down in the heart of the coals. Then you sit, and you go still, and you meditate while the fire works.

Time runs out long and quiet by the water. The pyre eats its fuel and the metal drinks the fire, and one by one you feel them come up to full — a low chorus of charged ember all around you, every battery topped, the mace heavy with heat again, the Furnace-heart a small banked sun. And you fill too: the cool well of your focus rising back to its brim, the ache going out of your limbs, the last of the cold-burn from before closed over and gone. When you open your eyes the fuel is spent to ash and the fire is sinking, but you are whole and brimming and surrounded by charged iron, gathered and ready in the warm dark by the cistern — and the long black shaft of the next floor is still up there, waiting, whenever you choose to rise.

You are rested, and every piece of iron you own is brimming with fire, and you have a shape in your head you have been carrying since the forge-floor taught you what your hands could do. So you begin, and you do not stop until it is finished.

Burning Anger first — you take it apart. The mace that has killed for you since the cistern comes undone under your own ember and the hammer-head's blows: the dense steel head off, the long iron haft free in your hands. Then the haft and the ember rod that was once Cold Revenge — anger and revenge both, the two weapons you named in the dark down here — you lay them together and you weld them into one. This is where you find the white you could never reach alone: with all your charged metal feeding the heat at once, the seam goes past orange, past yellow, up into a white so bright it throws your shadow huge on the cistern wall, and the two iron lengths run together into a single shaft as if they had never been apart. The batteries pay for the fire your own affinity could not.

Then the head. You set the Furnace-heart at the center of it — the dead guardian's core, your deepest vessel — and you build the weapon's striking mass out around it, breaking down the rivet, the old brazier-stand that has held your every fire in this place, and Burning Anger's steel head, layering each one onto the core white-hot and beating it home, ring after ring, until the Furnace-heart beats at the heart of a maul like a banked sun in an iron fist. That head you weld to one end of the shaft. The forge-bound hammer-head you weld to the other. And all the while you spend yourself the way you meant to — pacing the fire out of your own core drop by drop, never dumping, never running dry, the well sinking lower and lower as the work climbs toward done, so that the last weld cools under your hands at the very moment the last of your focus goes out of you. Spent, exactly. Not a drop wasted, not a drop short.

You set the butt of it to the stone and stand back, and for a while you just look.

It is the finest thing you have ever made. Two-handed, double-ended, heavier than anything you have carried — a maul head with a sun in its heart on one end, a hammer poll on the other, the whole long shaft saturated with ember through every weld so that it seems to hold its own dim glow even quenched and cooling. Every battery you owned is in it now; every named iron you carried down here is in it now; the brazier that warmed you and the core you tore out of a guardian and the bar you bit the swarm with, all of it gathered into one weight balanced so true it feels lighter in the hands than it has any right to. It has no name yet. You will know the name when it has done something to earn one.

Then you sit, because the work is done and your well is dry, and you meditate one last time by the sinking warmth. The focus rises back in you slow and full, the ache leaves your arms, and the new weapon rests across your knees drinking the last of the ember it can hold. When you open your eyes you are whole and full and armed as you have never been — and there is nothing left down here to make, nothing left to mend, only the long black shaft of the floor above and whatever waits at the top of it, for whenever you decide to climb.

You travel light, because the Tower has taught you that what you carry should earn the weight of it. The two clouded eye-lenses and the cold river-stone go into your pockets — small strange things, kept for what they might yet have to teach you. The stalker's pale hide you shake out and tie loose around your neck, a rough cloak against whatever waits in the dark above; it is not fitted and it is not fine, but it turns a blow better than bare skin, and the dead hunter has no more use for it.

Then you take up the maul, and you stand a moment with the weight of it settling into your hands, deciding what to call this thing you have made. But the truth is you already know. It is a different weapon than the one you named at the bottom of the cistern — heavier, doubled, a guardian's heart beating fire where a plain steel head used to sit — and yet that very steel is still in it, folded into the new head, the metal that crushed the drowned thing carried up through every shape this iron has taken: bar, mace, conduit, and now this. The name has come up through all of it unchanged, because the thing at the core of it never changed — only grew. So you keep it. Burning Anger. Still. Always. You shoulder the maul, and it sits there glowing low and patient against your back like it has known its name all along.

You go back to the throat of the shaft and this time you do not stop at the lip. At the first landing you find what your scouting promised: a bracket-lantern and a flask of old oil, sealed. You fill the lantern and you do not bother with flint — you set a fingertip of your own ember to the wick and it catches at once, and for the first time the lower shaft has light that is not the far grey seam. The dark pulls back off the broken flights and the rising slabs, and the whole murderous geometry of the place lays itself out for you to read.

So you climb. The flights are bolted to the wall, solid where they hold and simply gone where they don't, and you take the gaps the way your legs have always wanted to take everything — a long step here, a driving leap there, your lower body doing what it is built for while the maul rides glowing on your back. Where the stairs give out the slabs begin, rising and sinking on the slow patient beat you watched from the lip days ago, and now that you can SEE it and you already know its rhythm in your bones, the timing is almost easy: you wait, you read the lift, you go — slab to slab, up through the moving dark, the long fall breathing cold under every jump and never once getting you. You are, it turns out, very good at this. You climb until the wall-stair is far below and a narrow stone ledge snags out of the dark ahead, and you swing onto it to breathe.

You are not the first to rest here. A man is on the ledge with you — or was; he has been dead a long time, dried and still, his back to the cold stone and a burnt-out hooded lantern gone cold in his lap. You take the lantern. It is a better tool than your open flame for what is above — it throws its light one way and keeps the glare out of your own eyes — and you wake it with a touch of ember and hood it down to a directed beam. He has no more use for it, the way the stalker had no more use for its hide.

Scratched into the wall by his shoulder, in a hand that goes ragged and then frantic toward the end, is a message:

  "To whoever climbs after — the stones do not move on their own. The thing at the top moves them. It sits in the chain and it sleeps, and the slabs are only its breathing; come near the grey light and it wakes, and there is nowhere up there to stand that is not inside its reach. I could not get past it. Three days on this ledge now and I am done climbing. If you mean to try — the weight is the whole of it, the chain and the drum it turns on and the catch that holds the—"

and there it stops, unfinished, the last stroke trailing off the stone.

You look up. Far above, past more rungs of rising slab, the grey seam of the exit is brighter now — and below it, where the moving stones seem to dock against something, the dark gathers into a mass too square and too still to be more shaft. You cannot make out what it is from here. But you know now that it is there, and that it is waiting, and that it wakes to the climb. The lantern burns steady in your fist. The slabs go up and down their slow beat. The ledge holds you, for the moment, in the middle of the dark.

You go up out of the dead man's ledge and you do not stop again. The hooded lantern throws its beam ahead of you, and the slabs come and go on the beat you have carried in your body since the lip far below; you ride them, leap to leap, patient and quiet, giving the dark nothing to hear. The wall-stair is long gone — there is only the moving stone and the long fall — and then the moving stone begins to change. The slabs slow as they near the top and dock, one after another, against a shelf of worked stone: a gantry, solid underfoot, the first still ground in the whole shaft. And there, at last, is the grey seam grown into a doorway — the exit-stair, close enough to see the steps.

Something fills the way onto it.

It sits across the only dock to the stair: an immense seated figure of fused stone and iron, taller than three of you, and the great central chain you have climbed alongside runs straight into it and winds around its middle. It does not move. It does not breathe. It is the thing the note warned of — the giant that is the weight. You hold still on the gantry's edge and you bring the lantern's beam onto it, slow, along the chain to where it wraps a great drum at the figure's waist. And there, in a pocket of shadow the open dark would never have let you find, the beam catches a single fat iron pin seated across the drum — a catch, holding the whole wound length of that chain against all its tension. The note's broken last line closes itself in your head. The catch that holds the weight. That is the whole of it. Everything this thing is hangs on that one pin.

You do not give it the chance to wake.

You set your feet on the still stone — the one thing this floor has refused you until now — and you draw the maul back, and the core wakes white in its head as you pull on it and on your own fire at once, everything you carry and everything banked in the weapon gathered into the swing. Then you bring it down on the pin with all of it: the mass of the maul, the wave tearing out through its head, your ember and the core's ember poured together onto that one seated catch.

The pin shears.

For half a breath, nothing. Then the drum lets go. The chain rips off it in a long scream of iron, all the stored tension of the whole counterweight unwinding through the colossus at once — and the figure comes apart from the waist outward, stone and iron flung wide, the freed chain whipping away into the black. The vast mass that was the counterweight drops out from under it and falls, and falls, and never once makes a sound. And below you, down the whole length of the shaft, the slabs sink one final time and stop.

The dark goes still. The beat that has tried to throw you into the deep since you entered is simply gone. You stand on a gantry that does not move, in a silence you have not heard since the arch closed behind you, the grey light of the exit open just past your shoulder. The warden lies in pieces across the stone — and among the wreck, where the chain tore loose, the heavy wound drum at its core has come to rest, and a long arm's-reach of the great chain with it.

You go back up to the headworks one last time, to the thing you broke. It is still now — truly still, in a way it never was while it slept; the great chain hangs slack off the gantry and the counterweight has settled into the dark below and will not rise again. The warden does not move when you climb over it. You take what the Tower owes you for the killing. The winding-drum — the dense iron core the whole murderous mechanism turned on — you work free of its cradle, and it is the heaviest thing you have carried out of any floor, a sullen weight that seems to keep turning a little after your hands go still. And a long length of the chain itself, struck loose at a worn link, heavy and cold and good iron.

Then you drag them up. The last rungs of slab are easier now that nothing moves them, and the grey seam of the exit widens as you climb until it is a mouth of pale light, and you haul yourself and your dead weight of salvage up and through it, and the long cold shaft — the dark, the dead climber on his ledge, the broken warden in its chain — drops away beneath your boots and is closed. Another floor under you. You do not look back down it.

You come out into warmth.

After the cold of the shaft it lands on you like a hand: a long, low, golden room, firelit and close and kind. A hearth is banked high at the far end, throwing soft light down a table laid the whole length of the room — bread, and dark meat, and bowls that steam gently in the still air — and chairs drawn ready, and at the head of the table a tall hooded figure rising to its feet as you appear, both hands opening toward you in welcome. "Come in," it says, and the voice is gentle, glad, the voice of someone who has waited a long time for a guest. "Come in, climber. You've come so far. Sit. Eat something, and rest — you're safe here. You've earned it."

You set the drum and the chain down at the threshold. And you do not step across it. Because everything the Tower has sharpened in you is, very quietly, screaming.

It is the hearth that gives it away first. You are standing near enough that a fire that size should be pressing heat against your face — and there is nothing. The flames climb and curl and the air off them is cold, and to you, now, a man whose whole body has been remade into an instrument for fire, a fire that throws no heat is as wrong as a voice in an empty room. And the moment you have caught that one lie the others come apart in your hands. The light has no honest source: the hearth and the lamps and the hooded host pour gold across the room and not one of them casts a true shadow, while your own body and the maul on your back throw theirs hard and black across the floorboards. The host's open-handed welcome — you watch it open again, and again, the exact same motion, a fraction of a loop in a thing wearing the shape of someone alive. And down the edges of that laden table, where the cloth hangs and the warm light thins, the pale shapes are not the legs of chairs. They are old, and they are bone, and there are a great many of them. And running under all of it, woven into the warmth itself, there is a pull — a soft, steady invitation to let your shoulders down, to set the heavy thing aside, to sit — and your will, tempered floor by floor, knows the exact weight of your own tiredness, and this is not it. This wanting-to-rest is being pressed into you from outside.

And it does not stop at this room. The warmth runs back past the hearth into spaces you cannot see from the threshold, and — this is the part that turns your stomach — it does not thin as it goes. It deepens. Whatever is being worked here is worked richer and kinder and more convincing the further in it reaches; this bright welcoming hall is only the shallow edge of something that runs back too far for one floor.

The host stands at the head of its table with its hands held open, patient, kind, waiting. The bread steams. The cold fire burns. The salvage sits at your feet on the threshold-stone, and behind you the way you climbed is still open to the dark.

You do not step across. You stand on the threshold-stone, the cold fire throwing its silent welcome at the back of your neck, and instead of going in you turn your attention inward — to the three hard points of unspent possibility the warden's death poured into you, still humming under your notice — and you pour all three of them, at once, into your WILL. Into resolve: the part of you that has climbed four floors of this place and never once let it tell you what to feel, never once mistaken its cruelty for fate or, now, its kindness for safety. You build that part of yourself up like a wall, deliberately, against the soft insistent hand pressing on you to sit, to eat, to rest, to trust.

And it answers. Your will sets harder under you, a floor you can stand on; the deep well of your focus goes deeper with it, steadied by the same resolve. The pull does not vanish — it is not a thing in you to banish, it is a thing being done TO you from across the room — but it meets something far more solid now, and breaks on it, and what was a soft tide trying to turn you becomes merely a pressure you are choosing, plainly and with your whole hardened will, to refuse. You are more yourself on this threshold than you were a moment ago, not less. The host stands at the head of its table with its hands open, waiting, kind. The cold fire burns. The way down behind you is still open.

You raise the two clouded lenses to your eyes, and the world goes strange. The warm gold of the haven — the light that has been pressing at you this whole time, soft and insistent and kind — DIMS, drains, drinks away, because that is what these dead eyes do: they swallow light instead of catching it. And as the false gold bleeds out of the room, what was always behind it stands through, plain and cold.

The hearth is dead. Not banked, not low — dead: a heap of grey ash with no ember anywhere in it, throwing exactly the nothing your own skin told you it was throwing. The long laden table thins to bare boards set for no one, the steaming feast gone to the grey suggestion of nothing. The pale shapes drifted along the floor that were almost the legs of chairs are bones — stacked, and dressed over, a charnel pile the warm light had been draping in gold. And the host, the tall kind hooded host risen at the head of the table with its hands held open to you — it thins as you look at it through the dark, the welcoming shape going translucent and hollow, an empty projected image with nothing inside it, a picture of a host hung in the air where no host stands. Whatever truly keeps this room is not the smiling thing at the table. The smiling thing at the table is a painting of a lie.

And you notice, looking through these cold lenses, that it is not only the room's false light they drink. The maul rides glowing on your back — and through the lenses its honest ember-glow is gone too, flat and dark; the warmth of your own fire, the one sense that has been your truest compass on this whole floor, goes black behind a dead hunter's eyes. These eyes show you the lie by eating every light there is — the room's, and yours along with it.

For half a breath, looking at the hollow haven through a dead predator's eyes, you feel something you cannot place: a prickle that the room is looking back — that somewhere far past this cold hall something deep has felt a familiar kind of gaze open in the dark and turned, a little, toward it, the way one hunter feels the eyes of another. Then it is gone, if it was ever there. The hollow host stands at its bare table with its hands held open, patient, kind, waiting — cold and empty and laid about with bones. The threshold is under your boots. The way down behind you is still open.

You don't go in. You stay on the threshold-stone and you make the maul into a longer arm.

The Warden's chain — the heavy length you struck free of the headworks two floors down — you lay one end against the butt of Burning Anger and call the heat up out of yourself to weld it, because the maul's own banked core still runs low from the climb through the dark and won't spare the fire. It costs you a little, drawing the weld-heat off your own kindled ember instead; but the join takes white and clean and cools hard, and now you have a maul on a chain — a head you can swing wide, and throw, and haul back. Routine work. Your hands know it.

Then you put it to use. You set your boots on the stone, keep your weight rocked back over your heels and behind the line — never once letting the work tip you forward across it — and you swing the chained maul around in a circle and hurl it into the gold.

And the gold hands you the lie, plainly, in the weight of the chain. The maul sails through the long laden table and finds nothing — passes through the steaming feast like a stone through smoke, no purchase, no catch, the dishes and the bread and the bright-poured wine parting around an iron head that does not feel them at all. It crashes on through the welcoming host at the table's head, and the host does not flinch, does not turn, does not so much as ripple: it stands with its kind hands open while a war-maul passes clean through where its chest should be, because there is no chest, because it is a painting hung in the air. You haul the chain back and cast again. Again it finds nothing. Again. The feast is light pretending to be supper, and your iron tells you so every time it swings through and feels only cold air.

It takes you many casts — the head skating off the bright lie, sailing through where solid things ought to be — before it finally bites on something that bites back. Something real, low and to the near side, under the gilded suggestion of the floor. You set your back against the chain with your boots still planted on the stone and you drag it out to you, across the threshold-line — and where it crosses into your own true sight the false gold can't follow it, sloughs away, and leaves lying plain on the cold stone at your feet what was always there: bone. Human bone, old and grey, a tangle of some climber who came up these same stairs before you and was welcomed in. The haven had it dressed in gold and called it a chair. You drag out more — a snarl of ribs, a long cracked thighbone — and snagged among them by a lucky catch of the hook, a snapped length of cold iron: a broken blade, pitted, a dead man's sword sheared off at a third of its reach. Real metal. You set it aside.

And while you work, the room answers you — not with a hand, not with a sound, but by trying harder. The welcome WARMS. The gold deepens and sweetens where you've torn the bones out of it, re-pouring itself over the gap, re-laying the feast, re-gilding chairs that were bones that are at your feet now and gone from the floor. The host's open hands lift a little higher, a little more insistent; the whole patient kindness of the place leans toward you over its bare board, as if to say, gently, that there is no need for any of this — that you could simply come in, and sit. The harder you pull the truth out of it, the harder it pulls to bring you in.

You stand on the threshold-stone with the chained maul recovered in your fists, a heap of cold grey bones and a broken blade at your boots, and behind them the haven glows warmer and kinder and more golden than it has yet — lying to you with everything it has. The way down behind you is still open.

With the bones at your feet and the haven still glowing its patient gold at your back, you crouch and draw the winding-drum core out of your pack — the dense iron drum you tore from the dead Colossus two floors down, still faintly humming, still somehow not finished unwinding. A plan has been turning over in your mind, and it turns on this one question: whether the force wound up inside this thing is something you can fold into what you already carry — into your ember, your bound metal, the way you have folded heat into every tool you have made.

So you feel it out. The iron itself answers you easily — sound, dense, the best stock you have pulled from the Tower yet, and warm where your hand rests against it; that warmth you read the way you read all heat, plainly, a familiar note under your palm. You reach past the warmth, then, for the hum — for the wound force you can feel is in there, coiled and patient and real —

and your sense slides off it.

It is THERE. You have no doubt of that; the drum thrums with it, a stored tension like a held breath, like a bow that has been drawn for a very long time. But when you reach to read it the way you read ember — to feel its shape, its charge, how it might take a bind — there is nothing for your sense to close on. It is not heat. You test it against the cold you know too, the opposite pole you have wielded and been refused by, and it is not that either: it does not fight you, does not bleed, does not push back against your ember the way cold does. It simply is not on any scale your senses are built to weigh. A force with no temperature — and you are a creature who reads the world in temperatures.

You sit with it a moment, the cold iron heavy in your hands, and you let yourself understand the honest shape of the answer. The metal is yours to work, gladly — the finest core you have carried. But the force inside it is foreign, a kind you cannot yet grasp with what you have. Whatever your plan wanted from this, it is going to have to wait on a sense you do not yet own. Behind you the haven glows on, warm and golden and patient, offering everything and meaning none of it. The way down is still open.

You take the chain — the Warden's length, welded to the maul's butt since the grapple — and you work your ember into it the way you have worked it into every tool you have made, binding the iron to your own pole so that it stops being a thing strapped to the weapon and becomes part of it, and so the weapon's well to hold fire runs a little deeper. It is your home element going into plain iron, so it takes and it holds, no question of that. But you work it rough this time — the essence going in wasteful, the join honest but inelegant — and it costs you more than a clean bind would, drawing down your focus and pulling the maul's already-low core lower still to pay for itself. When it is done the chain is ember, of a piece with the rest, and the maul will hold a notch more fire than before. But a deeper well is an emptier one, and you have spent to dig it.

Then you sit. Down onto the threshold-stone, the way back at your spine, the haven's gold pressing its endless soft welcome against you — and you close your eyes and you do not take one thread of what the room is holding out. Not the laid table, not the warm-seeming hearth, not the patient open-handed host. You turn inward instead, to your own banked fire and your own set will, and you meditate the way you have on every floor below this one: drawing yourself back toward whole from your own center, on nothing but what is already yours.

Your body answers. The deep ache of the climb and the long grapple eases, your legs unknotting, the well of your focus filling back up from your own steadied core. But not all the way. Here, still and quiet and turned inward, the haven's pull is a headwind you feel on the last stretch of every breath — not hauling you over, you will not let it, but leaning on you, working hardest exactly when you are most at rest, so that the final measure of wholeness keeps sliding just out of your hands. And because your will is set so hard against it, you read it even as it presses: you feel the SHAPE of the thing's hunger as it leans in, patient and starving and wanting, very much, for you to stop refusing. You learn something true about what keeps this place by the exact weight of how it wants you.

Then you turn that recovered fire down into the maul — pouring focus into the deepened reservoir, reaching to fill the weapon and yourself both to the brim at once. And you meet the wall of it. Every measure of ember you pour into the maul is a measure out of your own marrow; the bigger well you just dug drinks more than you can spare; the two needles climb toward full and you cannot make them both crest. You bank the maul to a moderate, working charge — real fire held, enough to channel hard when you need it — and yourself to near-whole, but BOTH, brimming, is simply not a thing this threshold will give you. There is no fire here to draw on but your own. The haven's gold is all light and no heat, cold as the lie it is.

And as you reach, half-aware, for any warmth that is not yours to spend — you feel it answer, faint and real: the winding-drum core in your pack, the dense iron still holding the slow-cooling warmth of the deep places, the one true heat within your reach that would not be coming out of your own bones. You mark that it is there. Then you let the meditation settle where it has settled, and open your eyes on the threshold — near-whole, the maul banked and warm in your hands, its chain ember-bright and one with it now. The haven glows on, gold and heatless and patient, leaning in.

You stand, eyes shut, and step across.

The warm gold that has pressed at you this whole time is simply gone now -- not dimmed, not fought, just shut out behind your own lids, irrelevant to a man who has stopped looking. What's left is what you can feel, and on a floor this cold that turns out to be a great deal. The heatlessness is everywhere, a flat dead evenness with no hearth in it and no living warmth anywhere, and against that nothing the real things stand out like coals on snow. Off to one side, where your eyes would have shown you a tall kind host with its hands held open, your ember-sense finds only a cold hollow -- a hole in the warmth shaped like a welcome, a void with nobody home. You walk past the picture of a host without slowing. It was never the thing in this room.

You go slow, the maul low and banked and ready across your hands, its chain ember-bright, your fire held coiled behind the head and metered out to a measured load -- a hard knock, not an emptying. And as you move deeper into the cold the other thing rises to meet you: that skin-crawl, the wrong oily prickle you've felt at the edge of this whole floor, only here it isn't at the edge anymore. It's real and it's close and it's moving -- a low rough bearing sliding through the dark with a hunter's patience, drawn to the blind man who walked willingly in, certain of its room and its trick and its easy meat.

It comes. The crawl swells against your senses, near and rising and about to spring --

-- and you don't wait to be sure. You loose the burst you've held the whole way in, straight through Burning Anger and out along the bright chain at the one real thing in the room, the maul throwing its banked fire in a single hard pulse of heat. You feel it land. You feel the skin-crawl FLARE -- a sick bright spike as your fire finds it and bites -- and then recoil, and then go out, snuffed in one blow like a candle pinched cold, the oily presence that filled the dark simply ending. The cold hollow where the false host stands does not so much as flicker; it never had anything in it to hurt.

The maul rides lighter and cooler in your hands, its deep fire poured down to a low banked coal. Your focus sits lower in you, spent but nowhere near dry -- you measured it, and the measure was right. The hall is quiet around you, gone still in a way it was not a moment ago, the watching weight of it lifted. You stand in the cold dark with your eyes still closed, the false gold pressing uselessly at lids you have not opened, and somewhere past this room the floor goes on down into a deeper dark you have not yet reached. The way you came in is still open behind you.

The quiet doesn't last, and you didn't expect it to.

You go on into it, eyes still shut, the maul low and banked in your hands -- its fire a small thing now, a coal where there was a furnace, but enough to read by. The dead hall opens out ahead of you into something longer and colder, a wider dark you feel more than picture, the heatless evenness of the floor running on and on. And the skin-crawl you came looking for is there to meet you. You wanted one more. You find more than one.

It is the same wrong essence the burst snuffed a room behind you, that oily predator-prickle -- but doubled now, or more than doubled, a low moving wrongness that is not in any one place. There is something off to one side of you and something else further round, and the sense of them slides and shifts, real and alive and patient, beginning to open apart the way two hunters open apart around one animal: one to hold its eye, one to come in from where it isn't looking. You feel them start to move around you in the cold.

And then the cold itself betrays you.

Heat. Warmth, blooming up out of the dark where there has been no honest warmth on this whole floor -- the haven has been cold gold and heatless light from the first step, and now, here, all at once, it is throwing heat at you, soft and bright and everywhere, washing in against the one sense you have been walking by. For half a breath it nearly turns you. And then the harder thing in you, the part that has not stopped reasoning behind your shut eyes, goes cold and certain: this heat is a lie. It is too sudden, too convenient, too exactly aimed at the sense you reached for when you closed your eyes. The place felt you cross the last room blind, by warmth and the lack of it -- and here it has learned to throw false warmth, to flood the very compass you switched to. The way of seeing that let you walk in the dark is being taken from you, deliberately, right here. That it is failing you is itself the answer: you have been understood, and met.

You reach for them through it anyway, and the fine edge is gone -- the false heat fills the dark the way smoke fills a room, and the real wrong things moving in it blur, present and unpinnable, more than one, you cannot say how many or quite where. They are closing. You stand undercharged at the mouth of a colder dark with your eyes still shut and two-or-more patient, hungry things drawing apart to take you from the sides, your blind way of seeing turned against you in the span of a single room. Behind you the cleared hall is quiet, and the way you came is still open.

You give ground, fast.

Not in panic — on purpose. You back toward the way you came, toward the narrowing neck of stone that drops back to the cleared hall and the threshold beyond it, and you make the dark work for you: out in the open gallery the two of them could come at you from two sides at once, the second sliding wide to take you from where you weren't looking — but a thing that wants to catch a man who is leaving has to FOLLOW him, and there is only one mouth back. You feel them have to give up the flank for the chase. The wrongness that was opening apart around you closes back into a line: one of them pressing close behind, the other crowding the narrow space at its back, both funneled into the single throat of stone you are giving them, because that is the only way left to reach you.

You let the near one close. You wait, backing, until the skin-crawl of it is almost on you in the dark — and then you stop giving ground and you give them fire instead. You pour a wave of it down the throat of the corridor, the heaviest you can raise on what you've got, a flood of ember filling the one narrow lane they have to come through. It doesn't matter that you can't see them; they have to be HERE, in this lane, or they don't catch you — and so this is where you burn. And it CONNECTS. You feel it bite something real: the near wrongness flaring up hard and reeling back, the one crowded behind it catching the edge of the flood and recoiling too, real essence searing under real flame — not the empty hollow gutter the false heat would give, not light pretending to burn, but the genuine sick flare of living things that have just caught fire. You hurt them. Badly, maybe. You feel them reel.

You do not feel them fall.

And there is no time to learn which. You turn your back on the burning lane and you RUN — and giving your back, blind, to something that fast is the price of leaving, and you pay it: a blow rakes across you from behind, the trailing thing lunging through its own scorching to reach you, and it lands hard, a deep tearing line of pain that nearly takes your feet. You keep them. You run through it, down the neck, across the dead hall where the keeper's ash still lies, and you throw yourself across the threshold-stone — 

— and the wrongness ENDS. Sharp, like a line drawn: the heatless gold, the false welcome, the skin-crawl pressure, all of it cut off clean at the door, unable or unwilling to follow you out. Behind you the haven closes over itself, its hunger banked back down to patience; ahead the honest cold dark of the shaft you climbed waits, known and indifferent. You are out. You are bleeding, and your fire is burned down low, and you did not clear that room — but you are out, and you know more than you did, and you are alive to spend it. The threshold-stone is under you. The way down is open at your back, and the haven is shut at your front, waiting for you to try it again.

You turn your back on the cold mouth of the gallery, and you go down.

It is not a retreat you are ashamed of. The skin-crawl thins behind you with every step you put between yourself and that re-cloaked dark -- the wrong oily prickle fading back to the edge of feeling and then below it -- and the further you descend the more your shoulders come down from around your ears. You know this stair; you came up it. The warm false gold lets you go without a fight, whatever the haven is it does not chase a man out its own front door, and the threshold line you crossed holds at your back the way it held before: a clean edge between the place that wants you and the place that merely is.

The warden's platform opens under you, and it is as you left it -- broad, bare, cold honest stone with no welcome woven into it and nothing alive on it but you. The thing that ruled this floor is gone by your hand, and the space it held is only a space now, wide and quiet and safe in the plain way the floor above can do nothing but counterfeit. You let the maul down off your shoulder. You let yourself down after it, your back to good solid rock, and for the first time in a long climb you stop holding yourself ready.

You are hurt more than you let yourself feel while it mattered. Now that it doesn't, the body sends the bill -- the deep ache of the blow you took on the way out, the scraped-empty floor of your focus, the heaviness sunk into your legs. You close your eyes, and this time it is only sleep. You let it take you.

And in sleep, your eyes work.

You are back in the welcome. The hall of soft gold opens its arms the way it did the first time, warm and bright and glad of you -- except the warmth is wrong now, wrong the way a thing is wrong in a dream: heat with no fire under it, gladness with nothing glad behind it. The host stands with its open hands. The light pools golden. It is all exactly as kind as it was, and in the dream you can see, where awake you would not let yourself look, that the kindness is a surface -- a skin of warm light laid over something the warmth is there to keep you from seeing.

There is a brightness off to one side, the way still water is bright, and your dreaming eye turns to it. Something looks back out of it. Not the kind host -- the thing the kind host is painted over, caught for half a sleeping breath in the bright cold surface, wrong and patient and nothing like the welcome it wears. You cannot hold it. The gold washes back in, the surface goes warm and smooth and lying, the host smiles its painted smile, and the dream forgets on purpose what it just let you glimpse.

But you do not, quite.

You wake whole.

It comes back slow and then all at once -- the cold stone beneath you, the bare platform, the lantern still burning steady where you set it down. You are mended. The ache has gone out of you, the deep tiredness has lifted, your focus has filled back to the brim -- a clean cold reservoir of it, ready to spend. The rest did everything rest can do. Your body is yours again, and full.

The maul is not. You take it up and feel it at once: the core rides low and nearly cold in the haft, a banked coal where there was a furnace, and sleep has not put one ember back into it. It is a made thing and not a living one -- it does not heal because you did. Its fire is gone where you poured it out a floor above, and it will not come back from nothing. It comes back from heat: fed in, held, given time. The lantern burns in its iron cage an arm's length away, small and steady and warm -- real warmth, honest fire, the one true heat-source you carry on a floor that only counterfeits it.

And you can feel, faint and far above you, that the floor you left has not stayed where you left it. Something in the warm dark up there has shifted while you slept -- resettled, re-warmed, smoothed itself back over -- the way a disturbed pool goes still again and gives no sign a stone was ever thrown. You cannot say what it means. You only know the haven above is not holding its breath where you wounded it; it has let that breath out, and drawn another.

You sit whole and rested on safe stone -- your focus full, your maul low, the lantern warm at your hand, and the cold climb waiting over your head.

You set the lantern down on the cold stone beside the maul, unhood it so its honest light spills out clean, and you sit.

This is not the threshold, where you had only your own fire to give and a heatless gold pressing all around that offered nothing back. Here there is real warmth in the world again -- small and caged and steady, the one true flame on this whole climb -- and you reach for it. You feel for the lantern's heat the way you have learned to feel for any heat, and you take hold of it, and you draw it across the little gap into the dark core sunk in the maul's head. You are not making fire from nothing; you are only moving it, hand over hand, the lantern's burning into the cold reservoir of the weapon, and because the heat is the lantern's and not your own the work costs you only the carrying of it. The core drinks. You feel it warm and bank and fill -- low to a steady working glow, a held charge with weight to it again, enough to feed your fire-work from its own store and spare your focus when the next room asks for fire.

You do not fill it to the brim. The well runs deeper than it used to and the lantern is only the lantern; to pour the last of it in you would have to drink the light dry, and you need the light -- to see by, to shield your eyes by, for the truth it shows that the gold up there hides. So you stop while it still burns. The lantern sinks to a lower, quieter flame, dimmer but alive, and the maul rides warm and ready in your hands once more, banked to a solid moderate fire. It will do. It will more than do.

Then you try the thing you came down here turning over in your mind.

You take up the dense winding-drum core -- the heavy tension-wound iron you dragged out of the Colossus's wreck, the soundest weight you own -- and you lash it fast to the loose end of the chain, the end opposite the great head of Burning Anger. Now the weapon runs strange in your grip: maul at one end, dead heavy core at the other, the long chain slack between. You set your feet, you take the chain up near the core, and you begin to turn.

The maul comes off the ground and swings wide, and at full chain-length it is a different animal entirely -- a head of forged ember whirling out at the end of all that reach, the spin building on itself, the momentum piling up heavy and wide until it sings in the air a body's-width past where any sword of yours could reach. It is enormous. It is also very nearly past holding. The mass wants its own way; once it is moving it does not want to stop, and it drags at your shoulders and your stance, hauling you a half-step off your center before you set your heels and wrestle it back. The arc is huge and slow and stupid and you could not place it on a coin to save your life -- but you can feel, plainly, what it would do to anything standing in the wide circle of it. You stumble once, catch yourself, laugh short and breathless on the empty safe stone where a stumble costs nothing, and go again. A wild thing. A thing you would have to learn. But a real one.

And in the turning, with the core flung out and straining at the chain, you feel it -- the other thing in the iron, the one your fire never could read. Under the spin the stored force in the drum wakes against the motion, torquing and pulling in a way mere weight has no business doing, leaning on your turn with a will of its own that is not momentum and not heat and not anything your ember-sense can close a hand around. It is there. It is real, a deep wound-tight wanting sealed inside the metal -- and it is shut. Your ember slides off it the way water slides off oiled iron; reach for it as you might, there is no door. You turn it over in your mind as you turn the maul through the air, and the understanding settles cold and clear: the force is in there, and it will not answer you until you bind it -- truly bind it, the way you once made the ember yours -- and you have not done that, and until you do, it is only a very heavy stone on the end of a chain.

You unlash the heavy core from the end of the chain and let the maul lie. The dervish-thing was never quite the point -- it was the door you were knocking on. The thing you want is inside the iron.

You take the winding-drum core up in both hands, hold it against your chest, and you begin to turn -- not the weapon this time, but yourself, your own body wheeling slowly on the cold stone, the dense weight cradled and spinning with you. It is not a thing you reasoned out so much as a thing you felt your way toward: the force in this iron is a turning force, a wound and waiting motion, and you cannot grip a turning thing by standing still. So you turn. You match it. You make of your whole spinning body a question put to the sealed tension in your arms, and you reach -- not with your hands, with that deeper sense, the one that has only ever known heat -- and you reach for something that is not heat at all.

And this time it is THERE. For the first time since you pulled this core from the wreck, the foreign force does not slide off you. You feel it -- truly feel it, catch hold of it with a part of you that did not know it could -- a vast wound stillness coiled in the metal, a held breath of pure stored motion, immense and patient and real. The thing that was a rumor under your hands at the flail's end is a presence now, gripped, known. You have found the door, and it is open, and the turning force pours up out of the iron toward you.

You pull it into yourself, the only way you have ever taken an essence in -- the way you drank the ember on the first floor, into the meat and marrow of you, to keep.

It does not keep.

The force surges up into you and finds nothing in you shaped to hold it. You are ember to the bone -- tempered and single-poled and made, all the way through, to bank fire; and this is not fire. It rushes in and sluices straight through you like a flood through an open sluice, touching everything, sticking to nothing, and pours out the far side of you as fast as it came. For one staggering instant you are full of a power you cannot feel the edges of -- and then it is simply gone, run out through your hands, back into the iron and the air, and you have kept not one drop of it.

The backlash takes you sideways. The unspent force, refused a home, shoves back the way force always does, and your own spin turns traitor -- the world wheels hard, your stomach with it, and you stumble three lurching steps across the platform with your head roaring before your heels finally bite and hold you up. You stand swaying on the safe stone, breathing hard, the core dead-quiet in your hands again, dizzy and emptied and strangely, fiercely glad. Because you understand now, with the certainty of a thing learned in the body: the force is real, and it is reachable, and you can touch it whenever you choose. You simply cannot keep it in yourself. You are the wrong vessel. To hold this, you would have to build it a home outside your own skin -- to bind it into something the way you once bound the ember into iron -- and that you have not yet done.

You take the winding-drum core back up off the cold stone and lash it once more to the free end of the chain -- the same rig as before, maul at one end of all that iron, dead-heavy core at the other. But you do not grip it where you gripped it last time. Last time you held the core-end and flung the great maul out wide, and it was a wild and stupid thing, enormous and slow, hauling you a half-step off your center every turn. This time you take the haft up close behind the maul-head itself, the weight of it gathered against your hands, and you send the CORE swinging out instead -- the lighter end, the far end, the weight kept in tight where you can master it.

And it answers your hands. You set your feet and begin to wheel the core-end around you, and where the wide dervish wanted to throw you, this wants to be DRIVEN: the center of it held close, the whirling weight out at the chain's end skating in a tight fast circle that you turn, and check, and turn again. Your shoulders and your hips know this work -- the strength to drive the heavy thing, the quickness to catch it and change its line -- and turn by turn the circle tightens under your control, the core humming around you on its short leash, going where you put it and coming back when you call it. Not the elegant mastery of a thing long practiced; you can feel the rough edges of it still, the catches where your timing lags the weight. But it is CONTROL. Real, usable control. The wild thing has a handle now, and the handle is in your fist.

And there is more in it than your arms. As the core wheels around you, the new sense -- the foreign one, the one that woke on this very platform when you reached into the iron and the force poured through you -- opens quietly alongside the work, and you FEEL the thing inside the drum ride the spin. The sealed tension in it is not dead weight; it leans into the turn, wound and wanting, a stored push you can feel surge and slacken as the circle comes round -- and feeling it, you time against it, let the whip run with the force's own wanting instead of fighting it blind. It steadies the swing. A small thing, a partial thing, but real: the iron is easier to drive when you can feel which way it wishes to go.

You slow the core to a stop at last, breathing hard, the chain going slack and the weight settling, your legs burning pleasantly with the work. You have what you came for -- a flail you can actually wield, and a sense that helps you wield it. But standing there in the quiet with the dead core swinging gently at the chain's end, you cannot shake the feeling that you have only found the shallow edge of something. You have learned to FEEL the force and to ride it, to let it steady what your hands already do. And some deeper part of you, the part that learns things in the body before the mind has words for them, turns toward a thought it cannot yet finish: that to merely feel this force and lean on it is the smallest use of it -- that a man who could DIRECT it, bend it, spend it the way you spend your fire, would do far more here than steady a swing. You do not know how. Not yet. But you know now that there is a how, and that you have just brushed the near wall of it.

You go back down to the safe stone and you let yourself stop. No tricks this time, no experiments -- only the old discipline, sitting still by the lantern with the cold honest rock at your back, drawing yourself toward whole from your own center. The platform asks nothing of you, and so for a long quiet while you take everything back: the burn goes out of your legs, the cool well of your focus climbs to its brim, the spin-dizziness and the ache of days of work drain away. When you open your eyes you are full, and rested, and done preparing.

You climb back up to the warm gold mouth of the haven -- and this time you have a plan that does not depend on the one thing this floor keeps turning against you. The last time you went in blind by warmth and the lack of it, the place learned to throw false heat and flood the very sense you walked by. So this time you will not reach for it at all. You will not feel for where they are. You will make a thing that does not need to know.

You set the maul down and run your Ember out along the welded chain -- home fire into bound iron, the way it has always gone easy -- and the whole length of it wakes orange, the chain and the heavy core at its end kindling into a live burning thing, fed not from your own well but from the banked store in the maul's heart. It costs the core dearly; you feel the Furnace-heart sink toward low as it pours its fire up the chain. But when you take Burning Anger up again in the tight close grip and roll the core-end out into its first slow circle, it goes around trailing flame -- a wheel of burning iron a body's-width wide, turning at the end of your arms. Let them come kind. Let them come from the side. There is no side to a circle, and the circle is on fire.

You start to spin, and you start to walk, and you do not stop doing either.

It is the crudest, surest thing you have ever done in this place. You cross the warm gold room as a moving wheel of fire, the burning core howling around you on its chain in a flat hard circle, your eyes half-shut and your senses deliberately shut tighter -- not looking for them, not feeling for them, refusing the room every hook it has. The false warmth pours over you and means nothing to a man who has stopped asking the warmth anything. The kind voices start up at the edges, close and warm and wanting you to stop, to turn, to let them near -- and you give them the back of your attention and the front of the fire, and you keep walking.

Most of the circle meets nothing -- the flail sweeps through warm shapes that aren't there, gold light parting around burning iron the way it parted around your tether once, no purchase, no meat. But twice, three times, something real lunges in for the opening a turning man must surely be giving them -- and finds the wheel instead. You feel it connect: a solid catch, a body taking the burning core full across as it closes, the sweep flinging it back singed and reeling out of your circle before it can land the intimate killing thing it came for. They are fast and they are patient and they time the gaps -- one of them rakes you across the ribs in the half-beat between passes, a hot line of pain, and another glances off your shoulder -- but a graze is all the circle gives them, and a graze is not how these things kill. They need you stopped and trusting and still. You are none of those. You are a burning wheel walking through their room, and you do not stop, and you do not finish them either -- you simply pass, sweeping them back bashed and smoking behind you, and leave them the empty gold to be patient in.

And then the warmth changes under you.

You feel the far side of the room come up -- the way out you were walking toward, the place the gold seemed to thin toward an onward dark -- and you carry your burning wheel through it and out the far side, and you let the spin wind down at last, the core swinging slower and slower until it hangs smoking and dim at the chain's end and the fire gutters low. You stand breathing hard in a new quiet, the kind voices shut off behind you, your ribs stinging where they caught you. You crossed it. Whatever that room was, you are through it.

But you are not out. You know it before you know how you know it -- the air here is wrong in a new way. The gold is thinner, grudging, stretched too thin over something it can barely cover; the warmth has gone threadbare and cold at the edges, and the welcome that pressed so hard a room behind you is fainter here, as if whatever weaves it has less to spare this deep. It is colder ahead. It is more total ahead -- a wrongness that does not bother as much with being kind. You came looking for the way up and you have found only another threshold, deeper in, opening onto a dark you have not yet read and have, for the first time on this floor, chosen not to. The burning core hangs dead-low in your hands. The maul's heart is spent down to a banked coal. And the cold thing ahead waits to be walked into, or not.

skills.name: Ember Channel
skills.note: Projects Ember essence into held iron — the tip or a longer span — lending a heat quality to strikes. A deliberate invocation that must be set and held, not reflexive. Costs Focus to call up and sustain; more metal lit means more drain.

skills.name: Ember Burst
skills.note: Discharges Ember essence outward from the body in a wave of heat that sears and flings back what stands close. The pulse is meterable: a measured burst is cheap, a full emptying is costly and hollowing.

skills.name: Essence Infusion
skills.note: Binds elemental essence into matter — either transferring a charge from one item to another, or binding directly from one's own essence supply into an object. A matching element (Ember into iron) sets cleanly and holds; an opposite-pole essence (cold) binds crudely and bleeds. A bound charge persists until spent, and can be renewed.

skills.name: Ember Wave
skills.note: Throws Ember outward at range as a wash of fire — aimable but broad. Control narrows the wash somewhat; a tight concentrated stream is beyond its current reach. Costs Focus.

skills.name: Ember Siphon
skills.note: Draws ember and heat essence out of a source — through a contact or struck point — into oneself, bypassing physical shells. A large committed draw can pull a source's heat out entirely, leaving it cold and inert. Overflow near capacity risks self-burn.

skills.name: Ember-Tempered Body
skills.note: Channels ember-essence into one's own flesh to scour weakness and harden it. A clean temper sets permanent physical gains; a rough one burns the flesh without hardening it. Self-harm scales inversely with Vitality and with control precision. Costs essence, HP, and risk.

skills.name: Smithing
skills.note: Mundane metalwork — shaping, joining, and forge-welding metal with heat, hammer, and quench. Ember supplies the forge-heat. Crude tools limit the work to rough mass and joins; the quality of a piece scales with the skill.
